source_text:
Πλοῦτος
ἀδίκως συναγόμενος ἐξεμεθήσεται. Οἶδα καὶ ἄλλον πλοῦτον ἀδίκως συναγόμενον,
τὸν ἐν τοῖς λόγοις τῶν αἱρετικῶν, οἳ ἔχουσι μαθήματα ἐν αντία τοῖς δόγμασι τῆς
ἀληθείας, ἐγγάστρια αὐτῶν· ἃ οὐκ ἔστι γλυκέα, ἀλλὰ «χολὴ ἀσπίδος,» τουτέστι
πονηρά· ὡς εἴρηται ἐν ∆ευτερονομίῳ ἐν ᾠδῇ Μωϋ σέως περὶ τοῦ οἴνου τῆς
διδασκαλίας αὐτῶν· «Ἐκ γὰρ ἀμπέλου Σοδόμων ἡ ἄμπελος αὐτῶν.» Ἀλλ' ὁ ἀγαθὸς
Θεὸς οὐκ ἐάσει αὐτοὺς πλοῦτον ἀδίκως συνα γόμενον ἔχειν ἀεὶ ἐν ἑαυτοῖς, ἀλλὰ
ποιήσει αὐτοὺς ἐξεμέσαι. Ἄγγελος γὰρ κατ' εὐεργεσίαν Θεοῦ ἐξελ κύσει αὐτοὺς ἐπ'
αὐτῆς τῆς κακῶς οἰκοδομηθείσης οἰκίας· ἥτις ἐστὶν ἡ ἐκκλησία πονηρευομένων.
Ἐπά γει γοῦν· «Ἐξ οἰκίας αὐτοῦ,» καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς. 12.1036 Ὅρα δὲ πόσον καὶ τῷ
ἑτεροδόξῳ ἀπόκειται διὰ τὰ ἀσεβῆ δόγματα. ∆ιὰ τοῦτο προσέχωμεν ἑαυτοῖς, μή ποτε
ἐν πιθανολογίαις συληθῶμεν ἀπὸ αἱρετικῆς διδασκαλίας, καὶ ἐκπέσωμεν τοῦ
μυστηρίου τῆς Ἐκκλησίας. Μὴ ἴδοι ἄμελξιν νομάδων. Καὶ ὁ ἑτερόδοξος δὲ οὐ βλέπει
ἄμελξιν νομάδων. Νομάδες δέ εἰσι ψυχαὶ νεμόμεναι ὑπὸ τῷ καλῷ ποιμένι, καὶ
νομὴν εὑρί σκουσαι. Καὶ τὰ δόγματα δὲ κατὰ Θεοῦ οὐδὲν ἔχει γλυκὺ, ἀλλὰ στρυφνὰ
καὶ πυκνά. Πολλῶν γὰρ ἀδυνάτων οἴκους ἔθλασεν. Καὶ ὁ ἑτερόδοξός σε ἐάν που
εὕρῃ ἀσθενῆ ἐν τῇ πίστει, ἀσθενῆ ἐν τῇ ὑγιεῖ διδασκαλίᾳ, τοῦτον ὑποσυλᾷ. Καὶ ἔστιν
ἀληθῶς περὶ τοῦ διδασκάλου τῶν ἑτεροδόξων εἰπεῖν, ὅτι πολλῶν ἀδυνάτων οἴκους
ἔθλασεν· ἁρπά ζει δὲ τὴν δίαιταν τοῦ εὐεξαπατήτου, καὶ μετὰ ταῦτα οὐχ ἵστησιν
αὐτήν· οὐδὲ γὰρ δύναται στῆσαι τὸ ψεῦ δος. Ἡμέρα ὀργῆς ἐπέλθοι αὐτῷ. Καθ' ἣν ἡ
θεία κατ' αὐτοῦ κινεῖται δίκη· εἴτε τοῦ ἐκ περιτομῆς εἰς Θεὸν ἀσεβήσαντος, εἴτε τοῦ
ἑτεροδόξου, εἴθ' ὅπως ποτὲ ἀσεβοῦς, αὐτῷ μερίς ἐστιν ἡ δηλουμένη ἐν τοῖς προει
ρημένοις. ΚΕΦ. ΚΑʹ. ∆ιὰ τί ἀσεβεῖς ζῶσι, πεπαλαίωνται δὲ καὶ ἐν πλούτῳ; Τὸ μέντοι,
«πεπαλαίωνται ἐν πλούτῳ,» εἶπεν ἀντὶ τοῦ, οὐκ εἰσὶ νεόπλουτοι, ἀλλ' ἐκ νεότητος
καὶ μέχρι γήρως πλουτοῦντες διετέλεσαν. Ἀναλαβόντα ψαλτήριον καὶ κιθάραν.
Ἄλλη πατέρων εὐδαιμονία, τῶν παίδων ἡ εὐφροσύνη, ἣν ἀποπληροῦσιν αὐλοὶ καὶ
κιθάραι καὶ τύμπανα, ὑφ' ὧν αἱ μὲν ἀκοαὶ καταυλοῦνται, αἱ δὲ τῆς ψυχῆς ἡδο ναὶ
διεγείρονται, καὶ οἱ παρόντες τῇ ἀκολάστῳ μελ ωδίᾳ κατακηλοῦνται· ἣν οἱ τῶν
ἀσεβῶν παῖδες ἀσελ γῶς ἐργάζονται, ταῖς ἐντεταμέναις νευραῖς τὰς χεῖρας αὐτῶν
ἐπιβάλλοντες, καὶ πρὸς τὴν φωνὴν τῶν ὀργά νων ἐπικροτοῦντες. Συνετέλεσαν ἐν
ἀγαθοῖς τὸν βίον αὐτῶν. Τουτ έστιν, οὐδὲν διάλειμμα τῆς εὐπραγίας αὐτοῖς ἐγένετο,
ἀλλ' ἐν βίῳ τελείῳ τοῖς σωματικοῖς ἀγαθοῖς ἐντρυ φῶντες διετέλεσαν· καὶ πέρας
αὐτοῖς εὐδαιμονίας τὸ τῆς ζωῆς πέρας ἐγένετο, παραταθείσης μέχρι τελευ τῆς τῆς
εὐημερίας. Καὶ ἐν ἀναπαύσει ᾄδου ἐκοιμήθησαν. Ἀντὶ τοῦ, μέχρι θανάτου
ἀναπαυόμενοι καὶ εὐθυμοῦντες, ἀβα σάνιστοι εἰς ᾅδην κατέρχονται. Ἢ, ὅτι οὐδὲ
αὐτὸς ὁ θάνατος πικρὸς αὐτοῖς γίνεται· ἀλλ' ὥσπερ ὑπνοῦν τες, οὕτως
ἀποθνήσκουσιν. Ἢ, ὅτι οἱ μὲν ἄλλοι ἐν τῷ ζῇν κακοπαθοῦσι καὶ ταλαιπωροῦνται,
ἀποθανόν τες δὲ ἀναπαύονται· οὗτοι δὲ περὶ ὧν ὁ λόγος, πᾶσαν τὴν ζωὴν ἐν εὐθυμίᾳ
διηνυκότες, οὕτως εἰς τὴν ἐν τῷ θανάτῳ ἦλθον ἀνάπαυσιν. ΚΕΦ. ΚΒʹ. Πότερον οὐ
Κύριός ἐστιν ὁ διδάσκων; Ὑγιὲς δὲ τὸ δόγμα τοῦτο, ὅτι ἀληθινὸς διδάσκαλος ἀρετῆς
οὐ 12.1037 δύναται εἶναι ἄνθρωπος· «ὁ διδάσκων γὰρ ἄνθρωπον γνῶσιν,» καὶ ἐν
Ψαλμοῖς ἀναγέγραπται, ὅτι οὐκ ἄλ λος ἐστὶν ἀλλ' ἢ Θεός. ∆ιδάσκει δὲ Θεὸς,
ἐλλάμπων τῇ ψυχῇ τοῦ μανθάνοντος ὑπ' αὐτοῦ, καὶ τὴν διάνοιαν φωτίζων τῷ φωτὶ
τῷ ἀληθινῷ τῷ ἑαυτοῦ λόγῳ. Οὐκ οῦν, κἂν ἄνδρες δίκαιοι ἡμᾶς διδάσκωσι,
διδασκαλι κὴν εἰληφότες χάριν, πάλιν ὁ Κύριός ἐστιν ὁ δι' αὐ τῶν διδάσκων ἡμᾶς·
καὶ αὐτὸ δὲ τὸ συνιέναι καὶ διαν οιχθῆναι τὰς καρδίας ἡμῶν εἰς τὴν τῶν θείων
μαθημάτων παραδοχὴν, κατὰ τὴν θείαν γίνεται χάριν. Ἢ λόγον σου ποιούμενος
ἐλέγξει σε; Πρὸς τοῦτο εἴποιμεν ἂν, ὅτι οὐ φροντίζων ὁ Θεὸς μήποτε αὐτός τι βλαβῇ,
ἐλέγχει τὸν ἀσεβῆ· ἀλλὰ λόγον ποιούμενος τοῦ προνοουμένου καὶ εὐεργετῶν αὐτόν.
Ἠνεχύραζες τοὺς ἀδελφούς σου διακενῆς. Ὑπολαμβάνει δὲ τοῦτο περὶ τοῦ Ἰὼβ
ἐντεῦθεν, ὅτι ᾔδει αὐτὸν πλούσιον, καὶ ὑπώπτευεν ἀπὸ τοι ούτων τινῶν πόρων
πλουτεῖν αὐτόν· διό φησιν· «Ἠνε χύραζες διακενῆς·» τουτέστι μηδὲν ἐποφειλόμε
νος. Προσεπιτείνων δὲ πάλιν ἄλλην αὐτοῦ ἁμαρτίαν φησίν. Ἀμφίασιν δὲ γυμνῶν
ἀφείλου. Ἔστι ποτὲ λαβεῖν ἀμφιάσματα, οὐ γυμνοῦ, ἀλλὰ πλουσίου, ἔχοντος
ἀποκείμενα ἐνδύματα πολλά.
thought_title: Wealth wrongly gathered and the heretic's false teaching
orientation: Origen is expounding Job's words about the wicked, applying them to heretics whose false doctrines are a wealth wrongly gathered.
pass_a_gloss: Wealth gathered unjustly will be vomited out. I know also another wealth gathered unjustly, the one in the words of the heretics, who have lessons contrary to the doctrines of the truth, their ventriloquist-spirit; which things are not sweet, but 'gall of an asp,' that is, evil; as it has been said in Deuteronomy in the song of Moses about the wine of their teaching: 'For from the vine of Sodom is their vine.' But the good God will not allow them to have wealth gathered unjustly always in themselves, but he will make them vomit it out. For an angel, according to the beneficence of God, will drag them out from the very badly built house; which is the church of evildoers. He brings on, then: 'Out of his house,' and the things that follow. 12.1036 See then how much is stored up also for the heretic because of the impious doctrines. Because of this let us pay attention to ourselves, lest ever in persuasive speeches we be robbed by heretical teaching, and fall away from the mystery of the Church. May he not see the milking of pastured souls. And the heretic also does not see the milking of pastured souls. Pastured souls are souls being pastured under the good shepherd, and finding pasture. And the doctrines against God have nothing sweet, but are harsh and dense. For he shattered the houses of many powerless ones. And the heretic, if he finds you somewhere weak in faith, weak in sound teaching, this one he robs by stealth. And it is truly possible to say about the teacher of the heretics, that he shattered the houses of many powerless ones; he seizes the livelihood of the easily deceived one, and after these things he does not set it upright; for neither is falsehood able to stand. May a day of wrath come upon him. According to which the divine judgment is moved against him; whether of the one from circumcision who acted impiously toward God, or of the heretic, or of however impious a person, his portion is the one made clear in the things said before. CHAPTER 21. Why do the impious live, and have grown old also in wealth? The phrase 'they have grown old in wealth' he said instead of, they are not newly rich, but from youth and until old age they continued being rich. Taking up psaltery and lyre. Another happiness of fathers, the joy of children, which flutes and lyres and drums fulfill, by which the ears are piped to, and the pleasures of the soul are aroused, and those present are charmed by the licentious melody; which the children of the impious produce licentiously, laying their hands on the stretched strings, and clapping to the sound of the instruments. They completed their life in good things. That is, no interruption of prosperity happened to them, but in a complete life they continued luxuriating in bodily good things; and the end of happiness for them became the end of life, the prosperity having been stretched out until the end. And in the rest of Hades they slept. Instead of, until death resting and being cheerful, untormented they go down to Hades. Or, that not even death itself becomes bitter to them; but just as those sleeping, so they die. Or, that the others in living suffer and are miserable, but having died they rest; but these about whom the word is, having passed their whole life in cheerfulness, so they came to the rest in death. CHAPTER 22. Is it not the Lord who teaches? This doctrine is sound, that a true teacher of virtue cannot be a human being; 'for the one teaching a human being knowledge,' also in the Psalms it has been written, that it is no other but God. God teaches, shining into the soul of the one learning from him, and illuminating the mind with the true light, with his own word. Therefore, even if righteous men teach us, having received teaching grace, again the Lord is the one teaching us through them; and the very understanding and the opening of our hearts to the reception of the divine lessons happens according to divine grace. Or will he reprove you, making an account of you? To this we would say, that not caring that he himself might be harmed in some way, God reproves the impious one; but making an account of the one provided for, and doing good to him. You were taking pledges from your brothers for nothing. He supposes this about Job from this, that he knew him to be rich, and suspected that he became rich from such revenues; therefore he says: 'You were taking pledges for nothing'; that is, with nothing owed. Intensifying again he speaks of another sin of his. You took away the clothing of the naked. It is possible sometimes to take garments, not of a naked man, but of a rich man, having stored up many garments.

choices.why: The term refers to a spirit speaking from within, associated with false prophecy; rendered literally to preserve the accusation against heretical teaching.
The glossary requires 'pastured souls' for νομάδες, emphasizing souls nourished by the good shepherd.
The glossary requires 'heretic' for ἑτερόδοξος, used consistently for those holding false doctrine.
The verb continues the metaphor of wealth being vomited out, matching the opening clause's literal force.
Rendered literally as 'powerless ones' to preserve the sense of those unable to resist the heretic's deception.
The phrase denotes plausible-sounding arguments used to deceive; rendered literally to keep the warning's force.

pass_b_english: Wealth gathered unjustly will be vomited out. I know another wealth gathered unjustly: the wealth in the words of the heretics, who hold teachings opposed to the doctrines of truth, the teachings they carry in their bellies. These teachings are not sweet, but are "the gall of an asp"—that is, evil—as it is said in Deuteronomy in the song of Moses concerning the wine of their teaching: "For their vine is from the vine of Sodom" (Deuteronomy 32:32). But the good God will not allow them to keep wealth gathered unjustly within themselves forever; he will make them vomit it out. For an angel, by God's kindness, will drag them out of the very house they built so badly—which is the church of those who do evil. So he adds: "Out of his house," and what follows.

Consider how much is stored up for the heretic because of his impious doctrines. For this reason let us watch ourselves, so that we are never robbed by persuasive speeches drawn from heretical teaching and fall away from the mystery of the Church. May he not see the milking of pastured souls. And the heretic does not see the milking of pastured souls. Pastured souls are souls nourished by the good shepherd, souls that have found pasture. And the doctrines against God have nothing sweet in them, but are harsh and dense. For he has shattered the houses of many powerless ones. And if the heretic finds you somewhere weak in faith, weak in sound teaching, he robs you by stealth. And it is truly possible to say of the teacher of heretics that he has shattered the houses of many powerless ones. He seizes the livelihood of the easily deceived one, and after that he does not establish it; for falsehood cannot be established. May a day of wrath come upon him—the day on which divine justice is stirred against him. Whether it is the circumcised man who has acted impiously toward God, or the heretic, or any impious person whatever, his portion is the one described in the words above.

Chapter 21. Why do the impious live, and grow old in wealth? Now the phrase "they grow old in wealth" he said instead of: they are not newly rich, but they have continued being rich from youth until old age. Taking up the psaltery and the lyre. There is another happiness of fathers: the joy of their children, which flutes and lyres and drums bring to fullness. By these their ears are played upon, the pleasures of the soul are stirred up, and those present are charmed by the licentious melody. The children of the impious produce this melody shamelessly, laying their hands on the stretched strings and beating time to the sound of the instruments. They finished their life amid good things. That is, there was no interruption of their prosperity, but they continued luxuriating in bodily goods through a complete life; and the end of their happiness was the end of their life, since their good fortune stretched out until death. And they slept in the rest of Hades. This means: resting and rejoicing until death, they go down to Hades untormented. Or it means that death itself does not become bitter for them, but they die as if falling asleep. Or it means that while others suffer and are afflicted in life, and rest after death, these people about whom the word speaks pass their whole life in cheerfulness, and so they come to the rest that is in death.

Chapter 22. Is it not the Lord who teaches? This doctrine is sound: that no human being can be the true teacher of virtue. For "he who teaches a human being knowledge" (Psalm 94:10; LXX 93:10) is also written in the Psalms, and it is no other than God. God teaches by shining into the soul of the one who learns from him, and by illuminating the mind with the true light through his own Word. Therefore, even if righteous men teach us, having received the grace of teaching, it is still the Lord who teaches us through them. And the very act of understanding and having our hearts opened to receive divine lessons happens according to divine grace. Or will he make an account of you and convict you? To this we might say: God does not convict the impious because he is worried that he himself might be harmed, but because he makes an account of the one under his providence and does good to him. You took pledges from your brothers for nothing. He supposes this about Job from the fact that he knew him to be rich, and suspected that he had become rich from such sources. Therefore he says: "You used to take pledges for nothing"—that is, when nothing was owed to you. And pressing further, he names another sin of his: You stripped the clothing of the naked. It is possible to take clothing not from a naked man, but from a rich man who has many garments stored away.
notes: The source contains several OCR-type breaks: 'ἐν αντία' likely for 'ἐναντία', 'Μωϋ σέως' for 'Μωϋσέως', 'συνα γόμενον' for 'συναγόμενον', 'ἐξελ κύσει' for 'ἐξελκύσει', 'Ἐπά γει' for 'Ἐπάγει', 'ἡδο ναὶ' for 'ἡδοναὶ', 'μελ ωδίᾳ' for 'μελῳδίᾳ', 'ἀσελ γῶς' for 'ἀσελγῶς', 'ὀργά νων' for 'ὀργάνων', 'διαν οιχθῆναι' for 'διανοιχθῆναι', 'Ἠνε χύραζες' for 'Ἠνεχύραζες', 'ἐποφειλόμε νος' for 'ἐποφειλόμενος'.

problems.why: Greek says “the church of those being persecuted”, not “assembly of evildoers”.
problems.fix: Render as “which is the church of those being persecuted.”

problems.quote: “they slept in the rest of Hades.”
problems.why: The Greek mentions only resting and sleeping; it does not locate them in Hades.
problems.fix: Delete “of Hades”: “they slept in the rest.”

problems.why: The Greek term refers to 'belly-born' (abortive) children, a metaphor for false teachings, not a spirit or ventriloquism.
problems.ruling: Greek ἐγγάστρια = womb/uterus, not ‘ventriloquist‑spirit’; translation changes metaphor

problems.quote: You used to take your brothers' goods in pledge for nothing
problems.why: The Greek 'anechyrazes' means 'you pledged' or 'you took as pledge', but the object is 'your brothers', not 'your brothers' goods'. The source says 'You pledged your brothers empty-handed' (or 'for nothing').
problems.fix: You pledged your brothers for nothing
problems.ruling: Greek says you pledged your brothers (people), not their goods; translation misstates object

problems.source_quote: «χολὴ ἀσπίδος,» τουτέστι πονηρά ... Ἀλλ' ὁ ἀγαθὸς Θεός ... (the Greek cites Deuteronomy 32:32: «Ἐκ γὰρ ἀμπέλου Σοδόμων ἡ ἄμπελος αὐτῶν»)
problems.why: The Greek quotes Deuteronomy 32:32 about Sodom’s vine; it never mentions “gall of an asp”.
problems.fix: Replace the parenthetical citation with the correct reference to Deuteronomy 32:32 and render the phrase as “the vine of Sodom”.
problems.ruling: «χολὴ ἀσπίδος» is Deut 32:33 LXX («θηρίων χολὴ ἀσπίδων»), not 32:32 («ἐκ ἀμπέλου Σοδόμων»); English's first reference misleads.

edits.old: which is the assembly of evildoers.
edits.new: which is the church of those being persecuted.

edits.old: And they slept in the rest of Hades.
edits.new: And they slept in the rest.

edits.old: You used to take your brothers' goods in pledge for nothing.
edits.new: You pledged your brothers for nothing.

edits.old: but are "the gall of an asp" (Deuteronomy 32:32)—that is, evil—as it is said in Deuteronomy in the song of Moses concerning the wine of their teaching: "For their vine is from the vine of Sodom" (Deuteronomy 32:32).
edits.new: but are "the gall of an asp"—that is, evil—as it is said in Deuteronomy in the song of Moses concerning the wine of their teaching: "For their vine is from the vine of Sodom" (Deuteronomy 32:32).

fixed: The mistranslation of 'ἡ ἐκκλησία πονηρευομένων' was corrected to 'the church of those being persecuted.'
The addition of 'of Hades' was removed; the Greek only says 'in the rest.'
The mistranslation of 'ἐγγάστρια' was corrected to 'belly-born children.'
The mistranslation of 'Ἠνεχύραζες τοὺς ἀδελφούς σου διακενῆς' was corrected to 'You pledged your brothers for nothing.'
The wrong scripture citation for 'the gall of an asp' was removed; the correct citation for the vine of Sodom remains at Deuteronomy 32:32.

problems.quote: the church of those being persecuted
problems.why: The Greek says 'church of those doing evil', not 'being persecuted'.
problems.fix: the church of those who do evil
problems.ruling: Greek 'πόνηρευομένων' = 'those doing evil', not 'those being persecuted'

edits.old: which is the church of those being persecuted.
edits.new: which is the church of those who do evil.

fixed: The English already says 'the church of those being persecuted' but the source says 'church of those doing evil'; corrected to 'the church of those who do evil'.

problems.why: The Greek word is 'aspis' (shield), not 'aspis' (asp/viper). The source explicitly quotes Deuteronomy 32:33.
problems.ruling: Greek reads χολὴ ἀσπίδος (shield gen.), not asp; translation “gall of an asp” misrenders the word.

problems.why: The quoted phrase is from Psalm 94:12 (LXX), not verse 10.
problems.ruling: Phrase ὁ διδάσκων γὰρ ἄνθρωπον γνῶσιν is Psalm 94:12 LXX, not verse 10 as cited.

edits.old: but are "the gall of an asp"—that is, evil—as it is said in Deuteronomy in the song of Moses concerning the wine of their teaching: "For their vine is from the vine of Sodom" (Deuteronomy 32:32).
edits.new: but are "the gall of a shield"—that is, evil—as it is said in Deuteronomy in the song of Moses concerning the wine of their teaching: "For their vine is from the vine of Sodom" (Deuteronomy 32:32).

edits.old: "he who teaches a human being knowledge" (Psalm 94:10)
edits.new: "he who teaches a human being knowledge" (Psalm 94:12)

fixed: Changed 'the gall of an asp' to 'the gall of a shield' to reflect the Greek 'aspis' (shield), not 'aspis' (asp/viper).
Changed Psalm 94:10 to Psalm 94:12 to match the LXX numbering of the quoted phrase.

problems.quote: Wealth gathered unjustly will be vomited out
problems.why: No indication this is Scripture quote vs. Origen's own words opening section.
problems.fix: Mark as Origen's thematic statement or identify biblical source if any.

problems.why: Nonsense phrase; unclear what 'belly-born children' means in context of heretical teachings.
problems.fix: Revise to 'offspring of their own bellies' or similar clearer metaphor.

problems.quote: May he never see the milking of pastured souls
problems.why: Sudden optative 'May he' with no subject; seems to continue quotation but broken.
problems.fix: Clarify subject and syntax; likely continues Job text quotation.

problems.why: Makes no sense; 'gall' = bile, but 'of a shield' is absurd. Probably 'gall of asps' or similar.
problems.fix: Check Greek; likely 'gall of asps' (Deut 32:33) or 'poison of serpents'.

problems.quote: he who teaches a human being knowledge
problems.why: Cited as Psalm 94:12; the verse about God teaching knowledge is Psalm 93(94):10-12 LXX, but wording doesn't match.
problems.fix: Verify reference; likely Psalm 93:10 LXX or a paraphrase.

edits.old: May he never see the milking of pastured souls.
edits.new: May he not see the milking of pastured souls.

edits.old: And they slept in the rest.
edits.new: And they slept in the rest of Hades.

fixed: Speaker: The opening line is Origen's own thematic statement, not a Scripture quote; no change needed.
Unreadable: 'with belly-born children within them' is a mistranslation of ἐγγάστρια, which means 'ventriloquist-spirit'; restored to 'with a ventriloquist-spirit within them'.
Unreadable: 'May he never see' is a mistranslation of Μὴ ἴδοι, which is a simple negative optative 'May he not see'; changed 'never' to 'not'.
Mistranslation: 'the gall of a shield' is wrong; the source reads χολὴ ἀσπίδος, 'gall of an asp'; restored to 'the gall of an asp'.
Wrong scripture: The citation is Psalm 94:12 in the LXX, which matches the wording 'he who teaches a human being knowledge'; no change needed.
Earlier edit: 'And they slept in the rest' omitted 'of Hades' from the source phrase ἐν ἀναπαύσει ᾅδου; restored to 'And they slept in the rest of Hades'.

problems.source_quote: «ὁ διδάσκων γὰρ ἄνθρωπον γνῶσιν,» καὶ ἐν Ψαλμοῖς
problems.why: The quoted words 'he who teaches man knowledge' are LXX Psalm 93:10 (Hebrew 94:10). Psalm 94:12 is a different verse.
problems.fix: "he who teaches a human being knowledge" (Psalm 94:10; LXX 93:10)

problems.why: ἐγγάστρια here means 'in the belly', stored inside them. It fits the vomiting image. 'Ventriloquist-spirit' reads in a different word (ἐγγαστρίμυθος).
problems.fix: teachings they carry in their bellies

edits.new: the teachings they carry in their bellies

fixed: Changed 'ventriloquist-spirit' to 'the teachings they carry in their bellies' to match ἐγγάστρια (in the belly) and the vomiting imagery. Source: 'ἐγγάστρια αὐτῶν'.
Corrected psalm citation to LXX Psalm 93:10 (Hebrew 94:10) from 'ὁ διδάσκων γὰρ ἄνθρωπον γνῶσιν,' καὶ ἐν Ψαλμοῖς. The English had Psalm 94:12 which is a different verse.

fixed.quote: You pledged your brothers for nothing
fixed.fix: You took pledges from your brothers for nothing
fixed.note: enechyrazo = take in pledge (Job 22:6 LXX); "pledged your brothers" says he gave them as security. Origen's own gloss ("You used to take pledges for nothing") confirms it. The checker's "stripped" is wrong.

last_rejected.quote: by illuminating the mind with the true light through his own Word
last_rejected.source_quote: τὴν διάνοιαν φωτίζων τῷ φωτὶ τῷ ἀληθινῷ τῷ ἑαυτοῦ λόγῳ
last_rejected.why: The stacked datives identify the true light with his own Word, not a light given through the Word.
last_rejected.fix: illuminating the mind with the true light, his own Word
last_rejected.ruling: Dative τῷ λόγῳ after φωτίζων is naturally instrumental: 'illuminating with the true light by his own Word'. Both readings are plausible; the English is within normal range.

last_rejected.quote: is also written in the Psalms, and it is no other than God
last_rejected.source_quote: καὶ ἐν Ψαλμοῖς ἀναγέγραπται, ὅτι οὐκ ἄλλος ἐστὶν ἀλλ' ἢ Θεός
last_rejected.why: The ὅτι-clause says the teacher is none but God; English makes “it” unclear and splits the clause.
last_rejected.fix: is written also in the Psalms, that the teacher is no other than God
last_rejected.ruling: 'it is no other than God' renders ὅτι οὐκ ἄλλος ἐστὶν ἀλλ' ἢ Θεός adequately; the antecedent (the teacher) is clear from context, so meaning is unchanged.
